items.body: That Porous Line follows as a deliberate shift—letting in just enough light to see differently without abandoning the dark corners they prefer to inhabit. Push For Night arrives here as a natural fit That Porous Line by Push For Night   Room40 has been one of experimental music’s most important and quietly consistent labels since Lawrence English founded it in Brisbane in 2000. Over 25 years and more than 300 releases, it has built a catalog that spans electroacoustic composition, musique concrète, ambient, and avant-garde sound art—releasing work from Ben Frost, Tujiko Noriko, William Basinski, Grouper, and dozens of others. English works from a home studio built beneath a storage room containing literally a ton of records, an apt metaphor for a label that operates under the weight of its own history while continuing to push forward. Push For Night arrives here as a natural fit.​ The duo of Oliver Chapoy—Brooklyn-based musician, producer, and engineer known for his work with Saxon Shore, Warm Ghost, and collaborations with Helado Negro and Mikael Jorgensen of Wilco and James Elliott, Louisville, KY-based and equally steeped in experimental and post-rock sensibility, began their collaboration in 2017 and have been slowly building a body of work that lives at the intersection of electroacoustic processing, collage, and abstract sound construction. Their previous Room40 release Lapsed Gasps was a dense, intense record built around Jon Mueller‘s archived percussion recordings, processed through heavy electronics. That Porous Line follows as a deliberate shift—letting in just enough light to see differently without abandoning the dark corners they prefer to inhabit. “It’s Sure To Be Dark If You Shut Your Eyes” is a standout. The drums and glitched phaser of what sounds like a rolling percussion or hit every 8 to 16 bars is beautiful to the ear. There is a lot of stereo panning at play with their sound elements throughout, and while there really isn’t any persistent melody taking place, this leans more toward sound play and effects stacking—how many effects can they layer onto the same overlying loop until it gets absolutely destroyed and becomes something else. That question is the compositional engine driving a lot of this album, and here it’s applied with precision rather than aggression. “Idler’s Reward” is another strong one as far as melodic content goes—its emotional build and three-part structure make it a compelling standpoint for emotional construction. The song has three distinct sections if you hear it that way. What sounds like a marking drum echoing in the background is ringed with delay and echo on particular instruments and synths, making it interesting to listen to as it unfolds. Right at the six-minute mark, a highpass filter is applied to a looping note being echoed as a beautiful clarinet, played by Zachary Koeber—emerges as the second section of the track, playing out until 7:39 where the third section arrives with no warning: distorted, filtered guitar chords coming in and echoing to their own death. It is a fascinating build piece that earns every minute of its eight-plus-minute runtime. “Bait Is Lowered” continues the album’s definition of itself as a collection of building emotional pieces. Another fascinating piece of sounds. The incredible thing about experimental ambience like this is how long you can keep the listener engaged with the sounds being created and fatiguing them with noise or drone. Halfway through this track there’s a disruption—what can only be described as if you took a drum beat and submerged it in a bucket of water and started washing it aggressively as it builds up with suds. The music is very much imaginative. “Turned Slowly And Slowly Turned” is another dark piece with very subtle coos and creaky electronic rolls simulating what sounds like electronic animals or chirps, separated into two distinctive zones, far away and reverbed out on one side, the subtle coos chirping consistently back and forth softly on the other, no effects on them but slowed. Distortion play at its finest. “Push For Night describes their process as decorating the cave and inviting specters to reveal a message, trying to catch something in the semi-dark.” ~J. Batista “That Porous Line” is actually a beautiful closer, not the one expected after listening to this piece, but one that sounds genuinely immersive. The concept and theme of the album is still present, the bizarre distortions remain, but the melodies are toned down. Towards the end of the track there may be recycled field recordings surfacing, not to the naked ear but the trained one would catch it. The overall listen is actually pleasing, which for Push For Night is itself a notable statement. This is fundamentally an effects album and it shows, in the best possible way. The structure of experimentation with guitars and ambience has come a long way from the post-rock tradition that both Chapoy and Elliott carry in their backgrounds, and what That Porous Line represents is those backgrounds fully dissolved into something that no longer resembles where it came from. Push For Night describes their process as decorating the cave and inviting specters to reveal a message, trying to catch something in the semi-dark. On That Porous Line, they caught more than they usually let go of, and the result is their most emotionally varied and accessible work yet, which for this duo still means strange, flickering, and lit by crepuscular light. That’s the appeal. That Porous Line is available on Room40. [Bandcamp] That Porous Line by Push For NightThe post Push For Night :: That Porous Line (Room40) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: “MASKARA / مسكرة” had been teased for months before Saint Levant released it as the lead single from his third studio album, AFANDI / افندي, a 12-track record pulling from the era of Arab pop icons such as George Wassouf and Kadim Al Saher. On the track, Saint Levant is joined by Mohammed Assaf, who built his name on his defining anthem “Ana Dammi Falastini,” which turned him into one of the most recognised voices in the region after he won Arab Idol in 2013. Assaf’s roots are tied directly to the 1948 Nakba: his mother’s family was displaced from Bayt Daras and his father’s from Beersheba. Born in Misrata, Libya, he grew up in Gaza after his family relocated there Saint Levant, born in Jerusalem, carries his own parallel history of displacement into the collaboration, most directly heard on “Deira,” a song named for his father’s hotel on the Gaza seafront that was destroyed in an Israeli airstrike. Built around straightforward Arabic pop, “Maskara” itself is a celebration of Palestine and the shared cultural heritage of both artists. It perfectly introduces AFANDI, an album Saint Levant calls an ongoing dialogue between past and present—designed to bring listeners back to the region’s musical golden age. items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — I'm a sucker for flashy weird cover art which in this case features some sort of giraffe-necked girlin the company of cyan backed stripes and bubble curlers. Add some wily angularity of classicUnivers Zero or Present based avant-prog and my interest is peaked. The Seattle based TROOT emergedfrom the band's namesake Tim Root who assembled a fiery chamber prog band that consists of 10musicians and takes a journey through the crossroads of classic chamber prog, avant-jazz and freeimprovisation. The band released its so far one off CONSTANCE AND THE WAITING in 2018 with anensemble that was handpicked from some of the most demanding and obscure underground acts in theranks of the experimental music universe.Root is the head honcho here and began his career as a classically trained pianist therefore thepresence of his piano-based charm is a dominant force throughout this album's six tracks with a 411/2 minute run. With 10 players on board this is the wonderful world of controlled chaos with theusual rock instrumentation of two guitarists, two bassists and a drummer along with the skronkyeffects of a saxophone and the expected chamber part of the equation in this case delivers by meansof the violin however there are ample offerings of an accordion adding some Mediterranean cafeelegance to the mix. While the star of the show is Root and his keyboard charming antics, the restof the band is quite competent delivering raucous avant-prog uprooting with the first two tracks"Axe For The Frozen Sea Within" and "Dance Elena" running the gamut of time signature frenzies atbreakneck speed to eerie atmospheric breakouts.While the album starts off on a high note, Root unfortunately steers things into a more pianorecital type of number on "Palasidai" which slows down the tempo and feisty knotty workouts severalnotches and rather serves as a breather that bucks the trend of atonal dissonance in favor of a moreballady even melodic piece that sounds a bit out of place although not bad per se. "Venice Of TheSky" jumps back into the avant-prog mind [%*!#]ery with stronger doses of jazz added to the mix andthe missing energy oomf that was missing from the previous track. And then another rather sleepyballad type of piano-based track with "Hollow By Footsteps" which sounds more like a 1950s jazzballad than anything that belongs on this album and IMHO the weakest track of the lot even if notbad if included under a different album mood setting. The album is redeemed by the knotty closer"Joey" which reverts back to the UZ meets Art Zoyd on steroids playbook and generates a scorcher ofan ending.Overall not a bad album save the two tracks that derail the momentum. Despite the furor of nastyavant-prog crafted on this album, the band unfortunately sounds a bit too close to its influencestherefore not really standing out as something unique and innovative although the band's excellentmusicianship makes this a very compelling listen nonetheless. It's not a perfect album due to thetwo lesser tracks that water down the whole album effect but even those tracks are not offensivelyawful in any way, just not suitable for what would make a cohesive album experience for me. Whilenot anything new under the sun at this point, the musical outfit known as TROOT nevertheless derivesan above competence level of crafty Rock In Opposition styled avant-prog that navigates an all-instrumental trajectory at least until the frenetic and unexpected screaming at the end of "Joey"which adds a nice twist to the tale. I do very much this band returns with a more adventurous albumbut despite the flaws this is still a very pleasant nerd out for those of us who love thisadventurous prog exhibitions of grandeur.

items.body: Review by tszirmay — Well, this album certainly pertains to the title, finding beauty and truth in musical form is a luxury that progressive rock can easily provide. Back in 2020 when leader Dave Bandana began this project, he immediately connected with some exemplary musicians, names like Peter Jones (surely one of the great British prog talents), American drummer Tim Gehrt, Welsh guitarist Gareth Cole and the illustrious Cosmograf Robin Armstrong (who left after the second album). The four mentioned though are still the core, firmly entrenched in heir own little universe, crowning their relationship with this splendid effort, as well as being their finest. Toss in wordsmith Brad Birzer, and the sterling lyrics come alive with profound poignancy. Nice expansive track to launch the listening experience, "Islands" has all the classic ingredients to make one lose themselves in an atoll of sonic pleasure. A heady combination of various stylistics seamlessly concocted to create escapism at its finest. Orchestral, Celtic, jazz, rock and folk tendencies unite as a common front, without any kind of tedium or overt simplicity. Initially silky smooth and ambient, the drama takes little time to divulge its many enjoyments, Gehrt's primal beat bashing along like a giant wave, Cole's tingling guitar behaving like a rudder, all captained along by Mr. Jones' exceptional storytelling voice. Like a sudden monsoon surging across the horizon, the latter's saxophone skills inject a sunny luminescence that can only make the heart race a tad faster. When the 'timeless' brass and axe decide to interweave, well, it is called magic for a reason! There goes my jaw again, fluttering away in the wind! I mean , WOW! Only a breezy pseudo-instrumental can express the willowing beauty of "Fallen Leaves", the numerous choral voices acting like foliage swept by Newton's discovery. Its brief yet arching voluptuousness and fragile pastoral sense evokes images of acceptance and serenity. An ideal set-up for the colossal wallop of "Arribabok", the suave Bandana bass underwrites the complete array of sophisticated sounds emanating from each instrument, proposing an almost funky vibe, yet Cole does experiment with Manzanera-like slivers from his insistent guitar and Jones does an extended Andy Mackay move on the saxophone. One can even detect a Paul Thompson sense on the drum kit. Proggy Roxy (my highest possible compliment)! Much like my very best friend Lazland, my favourite month is also October, being hopeless romantic Autumn fans me thinks, and on "October Sun", it's purely heartwarming in its utter innocence, verging on panacea for the soul of fall worshippers, 'until the sun shines through'. A hint of my all-time favourite album (Hero and Heroine by the Strawbs), what with choral mentions of shining and suns, the clanging Cole guitars even recollect fond memories of Dave Lambert. Thankfully, the Jones saxophone slams this into another jurisdiction as the jovial bass bops like a Mexican jumping bean (remember those?). My feet, my hands and my head were forcefully keeping the beat?.Fun times coming up soon . Speaking of which, "From Empty Trees" has a monstrous and trebly bass running rampant on this instrumental, the ebullient synthesizers slipping between the branches, organ unafraid to pomp as well as supply ceremony and finish of the proceedings with a scorching guitar solo just to keep the forest ranger faraway from Yogi Bear (let us not forget Bubu). Epic time to rejoice once again, "A View" offers an orchestral and rhythmic foundation for Jones to emote vocally like only he can. His ability to plead, to beg, to steal and to borrow in his various inflections is absolutely masterful. Every single vowel and consonant are clear as the water in that lagoon on that island, where this stellar journey began. Talk about escapism, I have been somewhere else since the very first note, very track a joyful paradise. "Harder to See" is next and it's hard to imagine that the overt atmosphere keeps glowing like a spiritual fireball , 'I sit and wonder! You have a plan and you can', believe you me! An inquisitive sentiment on the complexity of confusion, of misdirection, of illusion, call what you want, its only words. The lamenting backing harmony vocals showcase the despair. Being a prog archivist and having a ramrod strong memory of all my hundreds of concerts , "Rewind" seems to wander back to gentler times, as befits us old geezers who still feel comfort in a youth very well lived. There is quite the classic golden age of 70s Prog feel to this finale , a carefree time when labels were meaningless and overt criticisms wiped away by astonished eyes and ears, every occasion we walked into a record store or a concert hall. Even the smells remain vivid to this day. The empowering orchestral send-off with acoustic guitars, flutes and mellotrons in tow is plain orgasmic. Rael must be on a poster somewhere in the studio, its eerie and yet so utterly expressive. Perhaps it was due to the Fly on the Windshield. 5 faultless things definitely worth remembering (who, what, where, when and why)

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — Despite the fact that this is a reunion album in which the band performs cover versions of it's old material, it's always nice to hear Quidam music--and to hear them reunited with former founding lead singer Emilia Nazaruk (n�e Derkowska) is a real treat--even these 30 years later. The other founding members present from that wonderful first album from 1996 are guitarist Maciej Meller and keyboard maestro Zbigniew Florek--the two dudes who have been writing the bulk of the band's music since day one. My favorite song straight away is the gorgeous "Jesteś (w labiryncie myśli) / You Are (in the Labyrinth of Thoughts)"--a song in which Emilia proves how she's still got all the skills and talents that she put on display back in 1996. "One Day We Find" also avails itself with great power as Bartosz Kossowicz earns his place among the pantheon of great Polish prog vocalists.The album's best song, however, may be its beautiful finale: "Spotykanie" (7:32) Here we have a remake of a song that first appeared on the band's last previous album, 2012's Saiko. I always love it when Quidam (or any band from non-English speaking countries) sings in their native tongue. Here Bartosz and Emilia take turns and even back one another as well as dueting within a gorgeous soundscape of guitars, synth washes, piano chords, and lilting flute melodies over Mariusz and Maciej Wr�blewski's warm and comforting bed of hypnotic rhythms. Then there's Maciej Meller's wonderful soaring guitar solo in the sixth and seventh minutes before Bartosz, Emilia, and Zbigniew so delicately tuck us in (for a wonderful night of peaceful sleep). Bravissimo! Great ending song to a fine comeback album! (14.125/15)Bass player Mariusz Zi�łkowski continues doing his great job of filling the shoes of the band's previous bassists as does flutist Jacek Zasada filling an equally-important role to this band's traditional sound. It's so nice to have Quidam back and still going strong!

items.body: Review by XixoTheRock — After dissapearing for some time of social media, Cherc�n has suddenly come back with a single!Which our first sneak peek to their next album, which they have confirmed (via Instagram) that theyare working on.Cherc�n has gone acid rock, and I am enjoying it, a lot if I'm to be honest. The single still hasband's DNA embedded in it, which means it still has a heavy, energetic and vanguardist approachto music, luckily enough, they were able to balance that with good production, something which Icomplained about on my review to their previous LP. Something I'd like to point out is how thissingle is a little more mellow for a hard rock/acid rock track, do I complain? No, that is becausethe music is astounding and hypnotic, and more mature stylistically than their previous work.Something I do not accustom to analyze in my reviews is the cover art, If I'm not mistaken, the lasttime I did so was with "The bedlam on Goliath" by The Mars Volta (which coincidentally, seems to bea big influence for the band, specially Pe�a's vocal delivery). This cover art is an edited pictureof the surface of mars, taken by NASA during their reconnaissance missions during the 70's, it hascirculated the internet and sporadically gotten famous every few years. This picture is without adoubt, fitting for the concept of the track, which orbits around the concept of pareidolia, apsychological phenomenon which consists of the brain triggering pattern recognition and observing(usually) human faces where they are not present. Despite being fitting for the lyrics/concept, I amnot in for taking pre-existing pictures/plastic art works for sleeve art, I consider this practiceto be exhibiting of low initiative, therefore I am not excited about the cover art. Does this takepoints away from the single? Sort of, since cover art does not really impact the composition of thetrack, then I can look over this, but for prog rock, a genre known for it multimedia and grandioseapproach to art, it feels incredibly dissapoiting.Music wise, I consider this single to depart from Cherc�n's previous vanguardist, metal and fusionapproach, taking one which is much closer to acid rock and heavy prog. The track starts with a cleanmath rock guitar riff, the delay and compression being reminiscent of Rush's songs like "RedBarchetta" or "Different strings", being accompanied by a simple bass line, and after Pe�a's vocalsstart, we get our transition to our Hendrix and Rodr�guez L�pez's heavy riffs. The track has somesynthesizer riffs which are played with grace and intricate metrics, which are the the backbone ofthe psychedelic textures, they are slimy spots on our vision which make us feel like we're spinningaround. There are two transposed and dueling saxophones which are the texture that grounds us alittle from our trance to space, the mixture of Synths and Saxophone polymetrics/polyrhythms createa psychedelic eter which makes us feel like we are floating in a dimension of patterns and figureswhich are celestial, supernatural, powerful and colourful. The jarring, clean then heavy then cleanagain guitar riffs are what give the track it's heavy acid rock feel, they are frenetic, much moresimple than Cherc�n's debut album riffs but still quite interesting, specially tonally, they arereminiscent of Tool and The grateful dead in a lot of ways, one of which is it's repetitive butheavy patterns, despite being in 4/4 most of the time, the bass also acts much more like a secondguitar instead of a rhythmic instrument, much like Metallica's original bassit Cliff Burton'sapproach to his instrument. It is the mixture of psychedelic textures with heavier riffs and amoderately energetic drumming which separate this from Avant Garde Fusion metal and drives thesingle towards Acid rock, it is heavy, psychedelic, but yet balanced and soft. The feel o get islike I am swimming in a sea looming over the mysterious auroras of Saturn and it's moons, it'scaptivating and dreamlike, but the energy is what makes this track NOT be a boring mellow space rocktrack, which is what it could have become, controlled frenzy and moderate energy that doesn't reachaggressiveness is what makes this track unique, very much like what Jimi Hendrix would write orplay.I think it'd be redundant to mention the incredible musicianship and dynamic of the musicians, sinceI have already written about this in the past (check my Cherc�n's LP debut review if you areinterested in the Chilean scene!), so I will elaborate further on what improved frok their previousrecord, mistakes they patched. I'd start with the most important thing which is Pe�a's vocals, whichhad been buried previously under layers and layers of loud instrumentation and a very mumble likedelivery, Pe�a finally articulates his vocals much more and this makes it much easier and lessdraining to try to appreciate the lyrics and their relation to the instrumentation, while alsokeeping his energy that accompanies the instrumentation perfectly, his influences by Cedric BixleyZavala have paid off! The production has also improved significantly when compared to their previousrecord, it's much more clear and balanced, less reverberating and recorded with better equipment,this I theorize is due to the new financing and help from organizations such as the Chileangovernment via their ministry of culture. The musicians are already well trained, experimented andvirtuoso so not much more to say regarding this. Does the single have flaws their previous recorddid? I'd say Peña still doesn't articulate to it's fullest yet, despite it all, the single denotes asignificant improvement compared to their previous work.The lyrics certainly are interesting! They are spiritual, very spiritual if I have to be honest,focussing on transcendence from the mundane human body and reaching it's fullest potential, thisexplored through the lens of our relationship to the material world around us. Those who arefamilliarezed with German idealism and Descartes's thought will recognize the resemblances theselyrics have to key concepts of the record, such as the thesis and antithesis Hegel speaks about, orhow Immanuel Kant critiqued pure reason and the idealists thought of how we can't actually accessthe world around us if it's not through perception and subjectivity. This is while the single iscalled "Pareidolia" and why it leaves heavy vanguardism behind for an acid rock approach. I amparticularly fond of the closing line "Elijo el infinito" (I choose infinity), which sums andsynthetices the entire track astonishingly great.Overall, I'd consider this single to be a great example of how to write acid rock in the 21st Centuryand it certainly does promise us a great record from Cherc�n in the near future, leaving an openquestion before us, will Cherc�n be able to top the biggest Chilean prog and art rock bands of thescene with their next record? Only time will tell!

items.body: Review by alainPP — Andrew Latimer, guitarist of the legendary band Camel, releases his second album?a continuous, seamless suite that eschews strict timing in favor of serenity, atmosphere, contemplation, and memories."From The Vault" is a suite Andrew created to help him move past his health issues?drawing on more than just his archives. "Those Times" opens with an Eastern flair before shifting to a deep riff and Gilmour-esque prog vocals. It evokes memories of his last tour?hence the cinematic sound effects?and features an Indian-inspired detour with flute, djembe, monolithic keyboards, and strings; "Why did you Lie?" is the question posed. The guitar solo is spellbinding, with a neo-classical keyboard style from Pete reminiscent of Manfred Mann. "Isolation" offers a Western vibe akin to Knopfler, Rea, or even Chet Atkins?a Southern-style track that flows endlessly. "Heaven," co-written by Pete, stays true to the Camel sound with divine flute work; it is a love song whose freshness brings to mind the Electric Light Orchestra."Clock Upon the Wall" emerges with folk banjo and conventional pop instrumentation, alongside a distinct bluesy feel. "Railroad Tracks" features metronomic drumming, a gentle start, and Alan Parsons-esque keyboards?a lovely memory?though the vocal duet and repetitive, soft-pop sound become somewhat grating. "Dingley Dell" uses piano to capture the eccentricities of the hero from Dickens' *The Pickwick Papers*, while a Genesis-like air rises from the label's signature charismatic atmosphere. "Clouds" concludes with an instrumental section where the guitar shines, surrendering to ethereal keyboards?a solemn moment reminiscent of one of Queen's final tracks.Andrew Latimer releases this musical suite. Orchestral arrangements provide the symphonic touch needed to elevate tracks that otherwise feel more like demos or outtakes.

items.body: Two years ago I reviewed the first release in this series, a Mahler Ninth (Alpha, 2024 – review), arguing that many of Philipp von Steinaecker’s contentions for “period performance” Mahler were unconvincing. There is no need to rehash those points here. In the liner notes for this release, Steinaecker describes the scholarly work done to ensure that the Mahler Academy Orchestra’s playing (vibrato, bowings, articulation, portamento, and the instruments themselves) matches what Mahler worked with at the time of composition. Symphony No. 5 Amazon Presto Apple But the conceit that the instruments and playing techniques of Mahler’s time result in a more accurate and successful performance is wrong-headed. Ultimately, the point of any recording is its worthiness for repeated listening. The playing here is good, and we hear the scholarship in action throughout. I find this performance more convincing than the team’s Ninth, but as a Mahler Fifth it does not match, let alone eclipse, the performances from Tilson Thomas in San Francisco, Tennstedt in London, Chailly in Amsterdam, Abbado in Berlin, and Bernstein in Vienna, to list just a few. The scholarship is on display right after the opening movement’s trumpet fanfare: the strings play the first theme (track 1, 1’10”) with minimal vibrato, heightened articulation, shorter bow strokes, and added portamento. But it comes across as a lecture demonstration rather than a musical performance. Where is the numbed grief heard in the Bernstein and Tennstedt readings? Both conductors use articulation, vibrato, and a little portamento to conjure that grief, more successfully than Steinaecker does here. He keeps tight control throughout the faster middle section (5’35”), never letting the music feel as if it might go off the rails. Yet we have a piano roll of Mahler playing a transcription of this music in which he creates a wildness suggesting derailment is imminent. The composer wanted emotional extremes. Should that not be the goal of every conductor of this music? The second movement takes off at a fast tempo but again lacks that last ounce of wildness. The playing is impressive, but I doubt any composer would choose technical perfection over emotional expression. As the fury subsides, Steinaecker chooses a dramatically slower tempo that loses momentum, and too little is made of the cellos’ lament a few minutes later. After the chorale climax, the opening music returns, finally as unhinged as it should have been at the start of the movement. The Scherzo brings two interpretive issues into focus. Steinaecker sets significant contrasts of tempo, surely intended for a more impassioned reading, but all too often the slower tempos bring a loss of energy and momentum. Bernstein and Tennstedt adopt tempos just as slow, if not slower, yet the tension never slackens as it does here. There is plenty of character when the orchestra is not focused on scholarly point-making, but just as often the playing seems intent on demonstrating “authentic” differences at the expense of the music’s emotional arc. Philipp von Steinaecker. The Adagietto, chaste and sweetly sung, frustrates: in a reading intent on honoring what Mahler intended, the speed is too slow. Two Mahler disciples with distinctly different interpretive styles recorded this movement within three decades of the composer’s death. Willem Mengelberg’s 1926 reading takes roughly seven minutes, and Bruno Walter’s 1938 reading roughly eight. Both had heard Mahler conduct this music, and in a performance predicated on honoring Mahler’s intentions, surely Steinaecker (9’05”) should be faster, which would arguably suit his orchestra’s less resonant gut strings. In a reading so focused on point-making, this tempo feels willfully out of place. In the Rondo-Finale Steinaecker finally loosens the reins, and the orchestra clearly revels in playing this music at a driven tempo. At last I sense the energy and power missing from the earlier movements. Steinaecker’s Coda is perhaps the most compelling and distinctive aspect of his interpretation; it would certainly bring any audience to its feet. If only the same freedom and imagination had been applied to the earlier movements. While I found more to appreciate here than in the team’s earlier Ninth, I remain unconvinced of any greater authenticity, and cannot recommend this performance ahead of those mentioned above. items.body: My Life With The Thrill Kill Kult released its fourth studio album, “13 Above the Night”, on 7 September 1993 through Interscope Records. The album turns 33 this year. Buzz McCoy produced and wrote the album, recording at Ground Control Studios in Los Angeles with Fred Giannelli co-producing and Eric Stitt Greedy and Jay Lean engineering. “13 Above the Night” was the band’s first release for Interscope and its first album recorded with touring members Levi Levi on bass, Otto Matrix on drums, Trash Kavity on guitar, and Chicago house vocalist Shawn Christopher. Lydia Lunch co-wrote and sang on “Dirty Little Secrets”. Guitarists Bruce Manning and Luc van Acker also contributed. What is on ’13 Above the Night’ The original 13-track edition runs “The Velvet Edge”, “Delicate Terror”, “Badlife”, “Dirty Little Secrets”, “China De Sade”, “Dimentia 66”, “Final Blindness”, “Blue Buddha”, “Starmartyr”, “Electrical Soul Wish”, “13 Above the Night”, “Disko Fleshpot” and “Savage Sexteen”. A 1999 Rykodisc reissue added two remixes, “Blue Buddha (Master of the UltraFlesh Mix)” and “Electrical Soul Wish (Miss Hate Mix)”, as bonus tracks. The album samples dialogue from two films: “Disko Fleshpot” lifts spoken lines from the 1969 film “Midnight Cowboy”, and “Starmartyr” samples the 1976 horror film “Squirm”. The band toured the US from October to December 1993 in support of the album, with Machines of Loving Grace as the opening act. About My Life With The Thrill Kill Kult My Life With The Thrill Kill Kult formed in Chicago in 1987 around Groovie Mann (Frankie Nardiello) and Buzz McCoy (Marston Daley), building an industrial dance sound around samples, disco rhythm sections and B-movie and exploitation-film imagery. The band released its debut album, “I See Good Spirits and I See Bad Spirits”, in 1988 through Wax Trax! Records, followed by “Confessions of a Knife” in 1990 and “Sexplosion!” in 1991, before moving to Interscope for “13 Above the Night” in 1993. “Hit & Run Holiday” followed in 1995, continuing the band’s run of major-label albums before further releases across the 2000s and 2010s. My Life With The Thrill Kill Kult has remained active on tour into the 2020s, including a fall 2025 run reported in My Life With The Thrill Kill Kult announces fall tour ‘Delicate Terror: Part 1’, taking its name from a track on “13 Above the Night”, and a spring 2026 US run covered in Heavy Halo join My Life With the Thrill Kill Kult for spring 2026 U.S. dates.

items.body: Lacrimosa released its eleventh studio album, “Revolution”, on 7 September 2012 through Hall of Sermon (catalogue reference HOS 8030). The album turns 14 this year. Tilo Wolff produced the record himself. Spotify’s release metadata lists the album a day earlier, on 6 September 2012; Wikipedia and Discogs both confirm 7 September as the official release date. Wolff sang and played piano, bass and drum programming across the record, with Anne Nurmi on keyboards and additional vocals. Two guest musicians joined the sessions: guitarist Mille Petrozza of Kreator and drummer Stefan Schwarzmann of Accept, alongside guitarists J.P. Genkel and Henrik Flyman, drummers Arturo Garcia and Manne Uhlig, violinist Christina Grabka, and the orchestra Die Spielmann-Schnyder. What is on Lacrimosa’s ‘Revolution’ The album runs 10 tracks: “Irgendein Arsch ist immer unterwegs”, “If the World Stood Still a Day”, “Verloren”, “This Is the Night”, “Interlude – Feuerzug (Part 1)”, “Feuerzug (Part 2)”, “Refugium”, “Weil Du Hilfe brauchst”, “Rote Sinfonie” and the title track “Revolution”. The cover art depicts the band’s recurring harlequin mascot standing over debris, waving a flag. German magazine Orkus named “Revolution” its album of the month for October 2012, and Powermetal.de highlighted Petrozza’s guitar work while noting the album’s more direct songwriting compared to earlier Lacrimosa records. The album peaked at number 35 on the German album charts. About Lacrimosa Lacrimosa began in 1990 when Tilo Wolff recorded the demo tape “Clamor” in Germany, releasing the debut album “Angst” in 1991 through his own label, Hall of Sermon, which he founded the same year. Finnish musician Anne Nurmi joined in 1993, becoming Wolff’s permanent creative partner. The band’s early studio run continued through “Einsamkeit” (1992), “Satura” (1993), “Inferno” (1995), “Stille” (1997), “Elodia” (1999), “Fassade” (2001) and “Echos” (2003), moving from Wolff’s gothic rock beginnings toward the fuller orchestral and metal-oriented sound that later defined “Sehnsucht” (2009) and “Revolution” (2012). “Hoffnung” followed “Revolution” in 2015. After a run of years without new studio material, Lacrimosa confirmed a new album was in production, reported in Worldwide paper shortage delays release new Lacrimosa album and The legendary Lacrimosa is coming back with a new studio album, and it will be released this year after all!. That album, “Lament”, was announced in January 2025, covered in Lacrimosa returns with an all new album: ‘Lament’. The band also released the double live album “Nachts” through Hall of Sermon, covered in Introducing ‘Nachts’: Lacrimosa Double Live CD on Hall of Sermon.

items.body: Gary Numan, the English synth-pop and new wave musician who had spent the previous two years fronting Tubeway Army, released his debut solo album “The Pleasure Principle” on 7 September 1979 through Beggars Banquet. The album turns 47 this year. Numan produced it himself at Marcus Recording Studios in London, with Harvey Webb and Rikki Sylvan engineering and mixing, and Julian Mills and Melvyn Abrahams mastering at Strawberry Mastering. The record arrived about six months after “Replicas”, his second and final album with Tubeway Army, and reached number 1 on the UK Albums Chart. How Gary Numan built ‘The Pleasure Principle’ without a guitar Numan dropped electric guitar from the sessions entirely. In its place he layered the Minimoog he had already used on “Replicas” with a Polymoog, leaning on that keyboard’s Vox Humana preset, an ARP Odyssey, and a Synare 3 for synthetic percussion. Flanging, phasing and reverb ran across the mixes, and solo viola and violin parts sat inside otherwise electronic arrangements. Paul Gardiner played bass, Chris Payne handled keyboards and viola, and Cedric Sharpley played drums and percussion. Billy Currie of Ultravox added fadeout violin to “Tracks” and “Conversation”, and Garry Robson sang backing vocals on “Conversation”. Side one of the original UK LP ran “Airlane”, “Metal”, “Complex”, “Films” and “M.E.”; side two ran “Tracks”, “Observer”, “Conversation”, “Cars” and “Engineers”. The sleeve took its title and its staging from René Magritte’s painting “The Pleasure Principle”, with Numan seated in the pose of the original but surrounded by artificial objects, including a glowing purple Perspex pyramid where Magritte had placed a stone. Tony Escott illustrated the cover, Geoff Howes shot the photography, and Malti Kidia art directed. First UK copies came with a printed inner sleeve carrying the lyrics on one side and a band picture on the other. “Cars” appeared as a single in August 1979, ahead of the album, and reached number 9 in the United States and number 1 in Canada. “Complex” followed that November and peaked at number 6 in the UK across a nine-week chart run. Numan later said he regretted the choice and that “Metal” should have gone out instead. Reviews at the time were mixed. Robert Christgau of The Village Voice described the album as “Metal Machine Music goes easy-listening”. Red Starr, writing in Smash Hits, called it “not bad, mind you”, but “much too similar” to “Replicas”. Record Mirror’s Simon Ludgate wrote that “detachment and distance are painstakingly sewn into every track”. Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark supported the UK leg of the tour that followed, a production built around banks of neon lights and two radio-controlled pyramids that moved across the stage. Beggars Banquet issued a 30th anniversary edition on 21 September 2009 with a second disc of demos, outtakes and live recordings, and a 40th anniversary set, “The Pleasure Principle: The First Recordings”, on 11 October 2019 across double coloured vinyl and 2CD. The album’s material has kept circulating outside Numan’s own catalogue. Nine Inch Nails covered “Metal” on “Things Falling Apart” in 2000, Afrika Bambaataa recorded it in 2004, and Basement Jaxx built “Where’s Your Head At” on “M.E.”. Side-Line covered a more recent reading of the same track in [melter] covers Gary Numan hit ‘Metal’ – Watch the video now, and the wider tribute traffic in Gary Numan revisited by various dark wave bands for a vinyl release – check the first video. About Gary Numan Gary Numan was born Gary Anthony James Webb in Hammersmith, London, in 1958. He formed Tubeway Army in 1977 as a punk band with his uncle Jess Lidyard on drums and Paul Gardiner on bass, and switched to synthesizers after finding a Minimoog left in a studio during the sessions for the group’s self-titled debut, released in 1978. The band’s second album, “Replicas”, came out in 1979 and reached number 1 in the UK, carried by the single “Are ‘Friends’ Electric?”, which also topped the UK chart. Numan dropped the group name that year, keeping Gardiner in the band and adding Chris Payne on keyboards and Cedric Sharpley on drums. “The Pleasure Principle” followed on 7 September 1979 and gave Numan a second UK number 1 album in the same year. “Telekon” arrived in September 1980 and did the same. He then moved through a long run of albums on his own Numa label and elsewhere, including “Warriors” in 1983, before his commercial standing in Britain fell away through the second half of the decade. The catalogue kept its influence regardless, and by the late 1990s a younger generation of industrial and electronic acts had begun citing and covering it openly. Numan’s later work brought him back to the same audience Side-Line reports on. “Splinter (Songs From A Broken Mind)” was announced in 2013, covered here in Gary Numan announces new ‘Splinter (Songs From A Broken Mind)’ album and tour – listen to first track!, and “Savage (Songs from a Broken World)” followed in 2017, reported in Gary Numan to release new ‘Savage (Songs from a Broken World)’ album on double vinyl (with 2 bonus tracks). He talked through his studio methods in Gary Numan – ‘After doing this for over 35 years I still get excited about what’s around the corner’ – Tech-Talk with DJ Wildhoney. Collaborations have run alongside the solo records. He worked with John Foxx on the release covered in John Foxx and Gary Numan collaborate on ’21st Century: a Man, a Woman and a City’ album – out in 2 physical versions, joined Jean-Michel Jarre’s “Electronica” project alongside Pet Shop Boys, appeared on a Chris Liebing album in 2018, and toured North America in 2023 in direct support of Ministry, as reported in Ministry announces 2023 headline tour dates with direct support from Gary Numan & Front Line Assembly. The Tubeway Army years were documented in the book covered in Gary Numan biography ‘Tubeway Daze: The Untold Story Of Tubeway Army’ hits the book shelves. Forty-seven years on, “The Pleasure Principle” remains the album Numan returned to most often on stage, performing it in full on dedicated tours in 2009 and again across the United States in 2010.

items.body: Siouxsie & The Banshees released their second studio album, “Join Hands”, on 7 September 1979 through Polydor Records. The album turns 47 this year. Nils Stevenson, the band’s manager, produced it with Mike Stavrou, recording at AIR Studios in London during May and June 1979. Ian Morais assisted with engineering. The album took the First World War as its lyrical starting point, after the band had watched televised scenes of repression in Iran and observed the two-minute silence marking the war dead in November 1978. The opening track, “Poppy Day”, set words from John McCrae’s poem “In Flanders Fields” against tolling bells; “Icon” and “Regal Zone” carried the theme further, the latter addressing the Iranian revolution. The closing track, a 14-minute studio recording of “The Lord’s Prayer”, reprised the song the band had famously performed at their debut show at the 100 Club Punk Festival in September 1976. What is on Siouxsie & The Banshees’ ‘Join Hands’ Side one ran “Poppy Day”, “Regal Zone”, “Placebo Effect”, “Icon” and “Premature Burial”, the last of which gave the album its title. Side two opened with “Playground Twist”, the sole single, followed by “Mother/Oh Mein Papa” and “The Lord’s Prayer”. Siouxsie Sioux sang and played piano, John McKay played guitar and saxophone, Steven Severin played bass, and Kenny Morris played drums and percussion. A 2006 remastered reissue added the non-album single “Love in a Void” and the previously unreleased instrumental “Infantry” as bonus tracks. Rob O’Connor designed the released sleeve, built around photography of four statues from London’s Guards Memorial, after Polydor rejected the band’s original artwork, a distorted Holy Communion card image designed by John Maybury. “Join Hands” reached number 13 on the UK Albums Chart and was later certified silver by the BPI. It was the last album to feature the band’s original lineup: McKay and Morris quit abruptly on the day of release, hours before a show at the Capitol Theatre in Aberdeen, and never returned. Siouxsie later described the record as reflecting the band’s state at the time: “We were lonely and isolated and that comes across in the music.” She added that “musically, Join Hands was an uncompromising album but it still sounds modern today.” Author Simon Reynolds has cited the album, alongside “Juju”, as a major source of gothic rock’s sound and lyrical themes. About Siouxsie & The Banshees Siouxsie & The Banshees formed in London in 1976, growing out of the Bromley Contingent scene around the Sex Pistols. The original lineup, with Siouxsie Sioux on vocals, Steven Severin on bass, and a rotating cast including Sid Vicious on drums for their debut performance, played “The Lord’s Prayer” as an improvised, 20-minute set at the 100 Club Punk Festival in September 1976. The band signed to Polydor Records in 1978 and released its debut album, “The Scream”, that November, followed by “Join Hands” in 1979. McKay and Morris’s departure on the day of “Join Hands”‘ release forced a rapid rebuild: Robert Smith of The Cure and briefly Budgie filled in on the resumed tour, and John McGeoch joined on guitar alongside Budgie on drums for “Kaleidoscope” in 1980, covered here in Siouxsie and the Banshees’ ‘Kaleidoscope’ turns 46 on 1 August. The band continued through “Juju” (1981), “A Kiss in the Dreamhouse” (1982), and the covers album “Through the Looking Glass” (1987), reaching a commercial peak with “Peepshow” (1988) and its hit single “Peek-a-Boo”, before “Superstition” (1991) and final album “The Rapture” (1995) closed the studio catalogue. The band disbanded in 1996; Siouxsie and Budgie continued as The Creatures. Siouxsie Sioux has remained active on Side-Line’s radar since, including a 2024 collaboration with Iggy Pop on “The Passenger” for a Magnum ad campaign, reported in Siouxsie Sioux and Iggy Pop collaborate on ‘The Passenger’ for Magnum Ice Cream ad – Out now, and former guitarist Jon Klein’s 2023 reworking of a Banshees classic with Jah Wobble, covered in Former Siouxsie & The Banshees guitarist Jon Klein teams up with Jah Wobble for a new version of a Siouxsie classic. Forty-seven years on, “Join Hands” remains the fault line between the band’s original punk-era lineup and the post-punk and gothic direction that followed.

Metropolis Records issued it in the United States on 10 September 2013. Eskil Simonsson handled vocals and composition, with Daniel Jonasson on keys and vocoder, Andreas Catjar on keys and guitar, and Joakim Montelius contributing lyrics and patterns. Daniel Myer, who had left the band’s studio lineup after 2011’s “Modern Ruin” to focus on his own projects, still co-wrote the opening title track with Simonsson. “Leaving Babylon” was Andreas Catjar’s first album with Covenant. What is on Covenant’s ‘Leaving Babylon’ The album runs 10 tracks: “Leaving Babylon”, “Thy Kingdom Come”, “Last Dance”, “Prime Movers”, “I Walk Slow”, “For Our Time”, “Ignorance & Bliss”, “Auto (Circulation)”, “Not To Be Here” and “Leaving Babylon II”. The record was released across CD, a limited digipak CD edition, and vinyl in Europe, plus CD and digital editions through Metropolis in the US. About Covenant Covenant formed in Helsingborg, Sweden, in 1986, founded by Eskil Simonsson, Joakim Montelius and Clas Nachmanson. The band’s early EBM and future pop sound, shaped by acts including Front 242 and Kraftwerk, first reached record through the 1994 debut “Dreams of a Cryotank”, followed by “Sequencer” (1996) and “Europa” (1998). “United States of Mind” (2000) and “Northern Light” (2002) extended the band’s international reach, with “Northern Light” carrying the single “Bullet”. Daniel Myer joined for “Skyshaper” (2006) and “In Transit” (2007) before those studio duties eventually passed on. “Modern Ruin” followed in 2011, and “Leaving Babylon” arrived in 2013 as the first Covenant album with Andreas Catjar in the lineup. The band’s next studio album, “The Blinding Dark”, was released in 2016 through Dependent Records, covered here in Covenant – The Blinding Dark (CD Album – Dependent Records) and in the release interview Covenant: “The Blinding Dark” – release interview and tour updates. Andreas Catjar-Danielsson, who played keys and guitar on both “Leaving Babylon” and “The Blinding Dark”, died on 29 July 2024 after a long illness, reported in Andreas Catjar-Danielsson (Covenant) has lost battle against cancer. Covenant later issued the charity release “Andreas EP” through Dependent Records in his memory, covered in Covenant charity release ‘Andreas EP’ out now on Dependent Records.

items.body: Ministry released its thirteenth studio album, “From Beer to Eternity”, on 6 September 2013 through 13th Planet Records. The album turns 13 this year. Al Jourgensen produced it with Sammy D’Ambruoso, recording between December 2012 and March 2013 at Jourgensen’s 13th Planet compound in El Paso, Texas. Dave Donnelly handled mastering. Jourgensen had said this would be Ministry’s final album, a plan later reversed with 2018’s “AmeriKKKant”. The sessions carried added weight: guitarist Mike Scaccia, whom Jourgensen described as the record’s driving force, died of a sudden heart attack three days after finishing his parts, while playing onstage with his other band, Rigor Mortis. Jourgensen and D’Ambruoso spent three months finishing the album afterward. Jourgensen recalled the tracking sessions themselves as smooth: “We have never, in the history of Ministry, ever had a tracking session like that before. Everything went so smoothly, it was surreal.” What is on Ministry’s ‘From Beer to Eternity’ The standard edition runs 11 tracks and 54:43: “Hail to His Majesty (Peasants)”, “Punch in the Face”, “PermaWar”, “Perfect Storm”, “Fairly Unbalanced”, “The Horror”, “Side F/X Include Mikey’s Middle Finger (TV4)”, “Lesson Unlearned”, “Thanx but No Thanx”, “Change of Luck” and “Enjoy the Quiet”. A Best Buy deluxe edition added “PermaWar Remix” and “Thanks for the Dub Remix”; the LP edition added a “Punch in the Face Remix”. “Thanx but No Thanx” sets William S. Burroughs’s poem “A Thanksgiving Prayer” to music, read by Sgt. Major, who had appeared on Ministry’s 2006 album “Rio Grande Blood”. Jourgensen sang and played guitar, keyboards and harmonica across the record. Scaccia and Sin Quirin played guitars, Tony Campos played bass on several tracks, and Aaron Rossi played drums. D’Ambruoso handled drum programming, synthesizer programming and co-production, and Aaron Havill contributed theremin, synthesizer and additional engineering. “PermaWar” served as the sole single, released through the iTunes Store on 9 August 2013. The cover art, by photographer Allan Amato, depicted seven models styled as sexualized, monster-like personifications of the seven deadly sins. It drew mockery from The A.V. Club’s Josh Modell, who compared it to Spinal Tap’s fictional “Smell the Glove” cover; Ministry responded with an alternate cover titled “Whole Lotta Glove” as a joke. “From Beer to Eternity” was also the first Ministry album since 2004’s “Houses of the Molé” without Tommy Victor on guitar or bass. The album reached number 140 on the Billboard 200 and number 7 on Billboard’s Hard Rock Albums chart. A remix companion, “From Beer to Eternamix”, followed on 22 November 2015. About Ministry Ministry formed in Chicago in 1981 around Al Jourgensen, mixing synth-pop on the 1983 debut “With Sympathy” before Jourgensen redirected the project toward the harder industrial sound that defined the band from “Twitch” (1986) onward. “The Land of Rape and Honey” (1988) and “The Mind Is a Terrible Thing to Taste” (1989) established the template of sampled vocals, distorted guitars and programmed rhythm that ran through the band’s most widely covered period, “Psalm 69: The Way to Succeed and the Way to Suck Eggs” (1992), which included the singles “N.W.O.” and “Jesus Built My Hotrod”. Jourgensen kept Ministry active through a long run of collaborators across the 1990s and 2000s, including “Filth Pig” (1996), “Dark Side of the Spoon” (1999), and a politically charged trilogy opened by “Houses of the Molé” (2004) and closed by “The Last Sucker” (2007), after which Jourgensen first announced the band’s retirement. He revived Ministry for “Relapse” (2012) and, after “From Beer to Eternity” in 2013, again for “AmeriKKKant” (2018), “Amerikkkant” follow-up “Moral Hygiene” (2021), and “HOPIUMFORTHEMASSES” (2021). Thirteen years on, Scaccia’s contributions to “From Beer to Eternity” remain the guitarist’s last studio recordings with the band he had rejoined multiple times since first playing on 1989’s “The Mind Is a Terrible Thing to Taste”.

items.body: ShiShi, the dark electronic project of Ljubljana-based artist Artur Ziganshin, released a music film on 1 September 2026. Titled “Blood Tape”, the 5:14 film is not a single or an album. Ziganshin wrote and directed it himself, and it is connected to his 2025 EP of the same name. The film uses vampirism as a metaphor for dependency. It follows a character whose private need gradually takes over his voice and identity. Ziganshin described the film’s arc as one where “fear becomes invitation,” invitation becomes hunger, and hunger “learns to speak in your voice.” The film is structured in six parts: Fear, Invitation, Hunger, Possession, Withdrawal and Void. “Blood Tape” was shot at 3840 x 2160 resolution and 24fps. Ziganshin handles the film credits himself: written and performed by Artur Ziganshin, with music and lyrics also credited to ShiShi. The film connects directly to the “Blood Tape” EP, a four-track release ShiShi put out in 2025 that includes the title track “Blood Tape” alongside “Doomnight,” “Rocket Ship to Hell” and “Storm Clouds Gather.” The film takes its title, and its central metaphor, from that release. About ShiShi ShiShi is the dark electronic project of Artur Ziganshin, an artist based in Ljubljana, Slovenia, who works across music and film. The project pairs original songs with visual work built around themes of fear, dependency, memory and transformation. Ziganshin writes, performs and directs the project’s output himself. Before “Blood Tape,” ShiShi released music including “Madness was Sad,” “Black birds” and “Sodium Crown.” In 2025, ShiShi released the “Blood Tape” EP, a set of tracks exploring dependency and confession through dense, cinematic electronic production. The 2026 “Blood Tape” film extends that EP’s world into a standalone visual narrative, translating its central metaphor of addiction as vampirism into a six-part cinematic structure.

The eight-track record is out now on digiCD, three years after the band’s previous studio effort. Eric “Doc” Hammer, known as a member of the American gothic rock band Requiem in White, produced “Theatre of Dust” and played drums on the album, the first time he has taken on both roles for The Spiritual Bat. The band describes his involvement in direct terms: “Doc gets it. Doc has the vision and the means to dress these songs for the occasion, while preserving our nature!” The album runs “Creatures”, “All My Power”, “Black Fields”, “Babylon Now”, “A Darker Gaze”, the title track “Theatre of Dust”, “Hello Heartache” and closer “Anti Matter”. An official video for “Anti Matter” is out alongside the album. Theatre Of Dust by The Spiritual Bat About The Spiritual Bat The Spiritual Bat is a deathrock and gothic rock band from Italy, conceived in 1992 by songwriter Dario Passamonti and singer Matteo Bracaglia. The project released a self-titled EP in 1993 under the name Spiritual Bats, followed by the band’s first full-length album, “Confession”, in 1996. The name later shortened to The Spiritual Bat, and the lineup has for years centered on Passamonti and singer Rosetta Garri. Further albums followed across the 2000s and 2010s, including “Sacrament” in 1999, “Through the Shadows” in 2008, “Cruel Machine” in 2011 and “Your Own World (And the Vision of Sound)” in 2017. The band signed with Swiss Dark Nights, which Side-Line covered as it issued an early single from the “Mission: Create” album in 2022, the same year the label also put out the retrospective boxset “Origins and Transmutations”, gathering material from the band’s back catalogue. “Theatre of Dust” continues that partnership with Swiss Dark Nights and marks the band’s first album made with Doc Hammer in the studio.

items.body: Claudio Simonetti’s Goblin reissue the “Tenebre” soundtrack on 18 September 2026 through Rustblade. The label presses a limited yellow smoke vinyl LP restricted to 499 copies, packaged with a replica of the original Italian cinema poster, alongside a digiCD edition that adds six bonus tracks. “Tenebre” is the score for Dario Argento’s 1982 film of the same name, known internationally as “Tenebrae”. Claudio Simonetti, Fabio Pignatelli and Massimo Morante, the three Goblin members behind the soundtrack, originally released it on the Italian label Cinevox in 1982. The score mixes early-1980s electronic dance and Italo disco elements with horror-driven progressive rock, built on vocoder vocals, electronic drums and pulsating basslines. The vinyl LP carries the original eight-track program: “Tenebre”, “Gemini”, “Slow Circus” and “Lesbo” on side A, then “Flashing”, “Tenebre (Reprise)”, “Waiting the Death” and “Jane Mirror Theme” on side B. The digiCD keeps that sequence and adds six further tracks, including a remix of “Flashing” by TIBIA and a cover of “Waiting the Death” by Simulakrum Lab, alongside alternate and live versions. Tenebre – Soundtrack by Claudio Simonetti’s Goblin About Claudio Simonetti’s Goblin Goblin formed in Italy in the mid-1970s around keyboardist Claudio Simonetti, guitarist Massimo Morante, bassist Fabio Pignatelli and drummer Walter Martino, after working under the names Oliver and Cherry Five. The band took the name Goblin while scoring Dario Argento‘s film “Profondo Rosso” (“Deep Red”) in 1975, and the soundtrack, released on Cinevox, established the group as Argento’s regular composers. Goblin went on to score Argento’s “Suspiria” in 1977 and, working with director George A. Romero, the soundtrack for “Dawn of the Dead” in 1978, released under the title “Zombi”. For “Tenebre” in 1982, Simonetti, Pignatelli and Morante reunited to compose the score, again for an Argento film and again released on Cinevox. Simonetti has continued to perform and re-record the band’s soundtrack catalogue under the name Claudio Simonetti’s Goblin, and has worked repeatedly with Rustblade on reissues and repackagings of the Argento-era scores, including the label’s past editions of the “Profondo Rosso” soundtrack. The new “Tenebre” vinyl and digiCD editions add to that reissue history with the film’s original score in a limited pressing.

items.body: Nina Hagen is working on a new gospel album, with release planned for Christmas 2026. The German singer confirmed the project during an appearance on the Cologne station domradio’s show “Meine Playlist”, saying the record was already in production. It follows her gospel-rock album “Highway to Heaven”, released on 27 March 2026 via Grönland Records. Hagen said the purpose of gospel music, for her, is “to get closer to God, closer to the gospel.” She added: “Black American gospel music, spiritual music, or even ancient church music – these are all entry points for me to get into conversation with Jesus.” Describing her approach to prayer, she said she expects, “like a child, without any ulterior motive, that Jesus listens to me, that it reaches Jesus, that I am there, that I am seen.” No title, tracklist or full guest list for the Christmas album has been announced. Hagen has not said which producer or musicians are involved in the new sessions, beyond confirming that work is under way. The upcoming record continues a return to gospel that has defined much of Hagen’s recent output. “Highway to Heaven” mixed Southern gospel, Americana and reggae with her long-standing punk energy across 14 tracks, and featured guest appearances from Nana Mouskouri, Gitte Hænning and Daniel Welbat. That album arrived 15 years after “Personal Jesus” (2011), her first gospel record, and marked her 20th studio album overall. About Nina Hagen Nina Hagen was born in 1955 in East Berlin. She rose to prominence in the late 1970s as the singer of the Nina Hagen Band, becoming known as a pioneer of German punk and new wave with a theatrical vocal style that spanned opera to punk shouting. After moving to West Germany, she built a solo career through the 1980s with albums including “Unbehagen” and “NunSexMonkRock”, and became a fixture of West German pop culture as a television personality as well as a singer. Hagen’s catalog has ranged across punk, new wave, pop and dance styles over the following decades. She was baptized in 2009 and released her first gospel album, “Personal Jesus”, in 2011, revisiting spirituals and gospel standards she had loved since childhood. She returned to the genre in March 2026 with “Highway to Heaven”, her 20th studio album, produced by Warner Poland. Side-Line previously covered the vinyl release of “Personal Jesus” for her 70th birthday. She is now preparing a further gospel album, aimed at a Christmas 2026 release.

items.body: Pet Shop Boys will release “A Man From The Future”, an eight-part work about British mathematician and codebreaker Alan Turing, on 9 October 2026 via Parlophone Records. Neil Tennant and Chris Lowe created the piece with Turing biographer Professor Andrew Hodges, and it can be pre-ordered now in several formats. The composition was first performed at the BBC Proms in July 2014 at London’s Royal Albert Hall, with the BBC Concert Orchestra, the BBC Singers and narration by actor Juliet Stevenson. For this new recording, both the text and the music have been revised and rearranged. Pet Shop Boys produced the album together with composer Sven Helbig, who also arranged the strings and vocals. The recording, made in the UK and Germany over the past year, features the Manchester Camerata Octet on strings and the Manchester Grammar School Choir, with Stevenson again narrating. The album is structured in eight parts following episodes in Turing’s life and work: “Natural wonders every child should know”, “He dreamed of machines”, “The Enigma”, “Other ranks”, “The memory and the control”, “The trial”, “Only in his death” and “A man from the future”. It will be released on vinyl, as a 2CD set and on Blu-ray audio, with the Blu-ray edition carrying the full sung-and-narrated version, an instrumental version and a version without narration in Dolby Atmos and 96kHz/24-bit stereo. Ahead of the release, BBC Radio 6 Music gives the new recording its broadcast on Sunday 4 October within Stuart Maconie’s “Freak Zone” (8-10pm), where Maconie also talks to Tennant, Lowe and Hodges about the reworking. The piece airs again that night on BBC Radio 3’s “Unclassified” (11.30pm-12.30am), with Tennant, Lowe and Hodges joining presenter Elizabeth Alker. Both broadcasts stay on BBC Sounds for 30 days. On 8 October, Tennant, Lowe and Hodges appear at the Imperial War Museum North in Manchester for a listening and conversation event built around a full playback of the album. About Pet Shop Boys Pet Shop Boys formed in London in 1981, when Neil Tennant, then a journalist at Smash Hits, met keyboardist Chris Lowe in a Chelsea electronics shop. The duo built up material through the early 1980s, first from Tennant’s flat and later in a small Camden Town studio, developing songs that became “West End Girls”, “It’s a Sin” and “Rent”. “West End Girls” reached number one in the UK and US in 1986, launching a run of albums – “Please” (1986), “Actually” (1987), “Introspective” (1988), “Behaviour” (1990) and beyond – built on Tennant’s deadpan vocals, Lowe’s electronic productions and lyrics that mixed pop hooks with social observation. Across four decades, Pet Shop Boys have continued to release studio albums, tour internationally and score stage and film work, including “Battleship Potemkin” and the musical “Closer to Heaven”. They are currently on their “Dreamworld” tour, for which Side-Line previously covered the announcement of the German support acts. “A Man From The Future” marks the duo’s first dedicated concept work built around a single historical figure, revisiting a piece they first performed with Andrew Hodges in 2014 and now releasing as a studio album on Parlophone.

Bektas wrote, performed and recorded “Vengeance” alone, crediting the cover art to himself, while “Possessed” was composed, performed, arranged, recorded and mixed entirely at Orko Productions in Sydney, with cover photography by Melike Bektas. Both tracks build slowly, layering horn-like synth tones and choral textures over an eight-minute run time on “Possessed” and just under six minutes on “Vengeance.” Possessed by Tir About TİR Oytun Bektas started TİR after moving from Türkiye to Sydney, where the project has been based since. Bandcamp and Rate Your Music list “Mountains” as TİR’s earliest full-length, released in 2016, followed by “Urd, Skuld & Verdandi” and “The Vanished Civilization of Xattoth” in 2019, “Nigritude” in 2020, “Persepolis” in 2021, “Awaiting the Dawn” in 2023 and the single “Sarcophagus” later that year. Orko Productions, the Sydney label and production outfit that mixes and masters TİR’s catalogue, has released the project’s work throughout that period. TİR has toured beyond Australia as well, including a show at Whammy Bar in Auckland, New Zealand, in July 2026, plus dates across Europe. Bektas has described performing at Prophecy Fest in Germany as “one of the most important recent milestones” for TİR. That festival history, along with the shows across Australia, New Zealand and Europe, sets up the “Southern Ritual” tour and the two new singles as the project’s latest chapter.

items.body: In an instant, your anxiety turned into fear. Every sacrifice needs an audience. In older ceremonies, the victim did more than die: one body was converted into communal relief, the crowd watched the exchange, and authority called the loss necessary. Modern systems rarely build stone altars, but the underlying bargain survives. Work, debt, status, and belonging keep asking for portions of the self until surrender becomes ordinary enough to pass for participation. Las Vegas K-Goth trio Past Self brings that bargain into view in their new video for 제물 / Jemul. Released during the band’s ongoing European tour, the clip was shot and directed by Kameren Isaguirre from a screenplay by vocalist and guitarist Sung Joo Kim. Isaguirre also edited the video and produced it alongside Past Self. The song’s premise treats contemporary life as a form of spiritual extortion: a social order that takes money, time, dignity, and private feeling in exchange for continued membership. Echo-heavy guitar figures hang above a steady rhythm section while Sung’s Korean and English vocals follow anxiety into fear, hallucination, betrayal, and ruined love. The music bears traces of The Cure and Lebanon Hanover, along with the broader dramatic scale of The Horrors and the saturated guitar mass of My Bloody Valentine, yet Past Self keeps each part legible beneath the distortion. When we first covered the single, the band explained its central metaphor: “제물 / Jemul translates to ‘an offering,’” says the band. “It refers to a society that constantly demands a piece of one’s soul as payment for being allowed to stay alive. The song aims to draw metaphorical ties between this concept and human sacrifices that a cult might make to appease their deities.” Isaguirre brings that concept to life in the song’s enigmatic and arcane visual. Sung appears among dry reeds and bare trees, his face painted white, his lips black, and his eyes sealed beneath a broad red blindfold. Dark stains spread across his loose white blouse as he carries a cloth-bound sword through the brush, raises it toward the sky, and performs with a red guitar. The blindfold makes him both marked victim and sightless officiant: he cannot see the spectators, though the camera is always watching him. A vast red disc glows behind a black field of branches. A single rose lies in disturbed soil, and the sword is planted beside it, turning the landscape into altar and grave at once. Elsewhere, a second blindfolded figure appears collapsed on a concrete slab before slowly rising beneath the final blue light of dusk. The images never settle into a literal execution. Instead, they suggest preparation, selection, and aftermath, leaving sacrifice as a role that can pass from one body to another. Night changes the video’s visual grammar. A severe blue-white lamp blows out faces and fabric as the trio plays in tall grass. Movement smears across the frame, bodies divide into doubles, and horizontal scan lines make the footage resemble a damaged transmission. By the final wide shot, a lone figure sits beside a small table among the weeds, reduced nearly to evidence. The altar described in the lyrics has become an anonymous stretch of land under surveillance. The red blindfold is the video’s most effective device: it blocks the subject’s vision while leaving him completely available to ours. In a song about society exacting payment from the soul, visibility becomes another fee. The victim may be unable to identify the crowd, but the crowd has no trouble identifying the victim. items.body: Strange to dream of you forever Even though I am wide awake The internet has abolished one of heartbreak’s few mercies: absence. Distance once allowed an attachment to lose oxygen, but the person we cannot stop thinking about now remains permanently available behind glass: photographs to revisit, timestamps to decode, and small signs of life that can be mistaken for an invitation to reminisce. Longing begins to resemble shift work, maintained around the clock by a thumb moving across a screen while the body waits somewhere else. That continuous state of checking and conjecture lies at the center of 24/7, the latest single and video from Pissoir des Dieux. The collaborative project brings together Larissa Iceglass of Lebanon Hanover, Vincenzo Wieczerzynski of Chaos International, and Owen Pratt of Uncanny Valley. Following their 2025 debut single, Hotel Grand Amour, the trio now announces their self-titled debut album, due September 28, 2026, through Fabrika Records. 24/7 begins with lightly strummed acoustic guitar and Iceglass’s breathy singing suspended in airy reverb. The arrangement is stripped down and emotionally exposed, carrying a bittersweet warmth without smoothing away its unease. Around the fifty-second mark, broad drums enter with a gentle crash as a thick, repeated bass figure gives the song a more regulated gait. Acoustic materials and machine-minded repetition begin working together, like an old mill keeping time at the edge of a forest. Near the two-and-a-half-minute mark, the bass drops into a deeper, slower, and more melodic sequence, turning the song toward something private and difficult to recover. It feels like watching an old home movie whose people can still move but can no longer answer. Bright guitar notes rise and fall through the closing passage, tracing small points of light like fireflies moving between the trees. Beneath that gentle surface, Iceglass describes attachment as a form of dependency. The absent person persists through photographs, clothing choices, questions about their safety, and even the condition of their keyboard; ordinary details accumulate until browsing becomes a self-administered dose. There is dry humour in the specificity, but it only makes the fixation feel more intimate. The phrase 24/7 becomes both a schedule and a diagnosis. Iceglass extends that idea into the video she directed and edited. Presented as grainy 4:3 camcorder footage, it carries date stamps for July 23 and July 24, 2025. Scenes from a birthday gathering at a country house—friends in the garden, rabbits in an enclosure, a dartboard, and an outdoor meal—alternate with close shots of Iceglass singing alone in a dim interior. At times her face is fully visible; elsewhere it appears as a pale fragment caught within a narrow strip of light. During the final passage, Iceglass leaves the house and enters the water beside a small dock, eventually lifting a glass above the surface. The footage possesses the factual appearance of a family tape, but its emotional status remains unresolved. It could be remembrance, fantasy, evidence, or the kind of saved material repeatedly replayed after direct contact has ended. The camera preserves a summer day with ruthless efficiency while the song considers what that preservation does to the person who cannot stop looking. Watch the video for 24/7 below: Pissoir des Dieux announce their eight-track self-titled debut album, arriving September 28, 2026 through Fabrika Records. Mixed by Owen Pratt and mastered by Schwebung Mastering, the record includes Hotel Grand Amour, 24/7, and six additional songs. Limited black, opaque, and pink vinyl editions are available, with each pressing limited to 500 copies. Listen to 24/7 below and pre-order Pissoir des Dieux here. items.body: Bands: Cocanha, Los Sara Fontán, Tarta Relena | Album: 4132314 | Genre: Experimental folk | Bandcamp This collaboration of three duos is a mixture of original compositions and reinterpretations of folk songs. Cocanha specializes in Occitan polyphony, Los Sara Fontán in Catalan folk, and Tarta Relena in electronic-tinged post-rock; and all three bands’ styles are on proud display here. The vocals are rich, multi-layered, and carefully arranged; and the backing is brimming with odd metrical flourishes. This record feels like it has one foot in the twenty-first century and another in the nineteenth, and it’s a fantastic mash-up. Score: 86/100 Band: Furii | Album: Pyromancy | Genre: Progressive pop | Bandcamp Furii (pronounced “fury”) is a Cardiacs-adjacent project, a fact which is unmistakable from this album’s opening moments. Sole bandmember Adrien Rodes is the longtime keyboardist of Spratleys (another Tim Smith project) and an occasional member of Cardiacs’ live band. Joanne Spratley, another member of Spratleys, provides vocals on Pyromancy, and her vocals lend an eerie, airy atmosphere. The textures on this record are psychedelic and dreamy, with tinkling piano and swirling synths. Despite the songs being rather to-the-point, the soundscapes presented are dense and complex, with lots of innovative sonic choices. I found LSD to be an exhausting listen (and not in a fun way), but this is a much more enjoyable spiritual successor to Cardiacs. Score: 80/100 Band: Godsticks | Album: VOiD | Genre: Progressive rock | Bandcamp Godsticks is a Welsh four-piece that plays a relatively heavy, alt-adjacent variety of progressive rock. This record is stuffed to the brim with flashy riffs, a rotating assortment of time signatures, and powerful vocals. None of the songs here are particularly long, but that focus pays off. Each piece features a powerful distillation of semi-metallic riffs and clever structuring. Quieter moments often feature some electronic embellishments, and I appreciate that tonal contrast. By the end of the record, things do start to sound a bit samey, but it’s still a solid release, overall. Score: 73/100 Band: Kaatayra | Album: Caminhos de Água | Genre: Post-metal, Progressive folk | Bandcamp This is a tough record to categorize with traditional genre labels. The band bills itself as acoustic black metal, and that really is the best summary, as odd as that sounds. Significant Brazilian folk influence is present here, as well. A friend showed me their 2021 album, Inpariquipê, and I thought it was interesting. My first impression was that it sounded like Incantations-era Mike Oldfield doing black metal, and I’ll reiterate that general impression here. Textures are lush, with various wind instruments and wooden idiophones lending sonic depth. This is an example of a record that, for me, at least, has benefitted from multiple listens. When I first heard it, I thought it was fine but I might need a little time to digest it. Each time I’ve come back to it, I’ve found something new to like or noticed some new intricacy I’d previously missed.  The album’s title (Portuguese for “Waterways”) is fitting, with the music here invoking rivers perfectly. There are moments of gentle relaxation as it flows and burbles. In contrast, there are moments where high-tempo rapids and waterfalls of anxiety and tension crash down upon the listener. Score: 87/100 Band: Slift | Album: Fantasia | Genre: Heavy psych, Space rock | Bandcamp Slift’s fourth LP sees them scale things back. My main complaint about Ilion was its crushing, unnecessary length. Fantasia features plenty of artsy, kraut-inspired riffage and soaring, interstellar textures alongside the band’s garage rock roots. But it’s presented at a much more manageable length. The emotion comes through clear as day in these songs, complementing the raw power of the compositions. Score: 81/100 Band: Spell | Album: Wretched Heart | Genre: Heavy metal, Progressive rock | Bandcamp The latest release from this Canadian traditional heavy metal quartet might be my favorite from them yet. In some ways, this record reminds me of Voivod’s Angel Rat, in that metal is often toned down in favor of psychedelia, prog-rock, and post-punk. The synth tones on this record also lend it a spooky, gothic edge, which couples well with the band’s smart and complex melodic passages. There are dazzling solos aplenty, and the songs’ constant morphing and churning keep the listener engaged. Score: 84/100
